Background and aims Inflammation plays a pivotal role in the pathophysiology of ST-elevation myocardial infarction (STEMI). This involves neutrophil activation and the local release of pro-inflammatory mediators. The formation of neutrophil extracellular traps (NETs) in coronary thrombosis has been linked to poor short-term prognosis following STEMI, but the usefulness of specific circulating NET components as prognostic markers is unclear. We aimed to evaluate the NET-specific marker nucleosomal citrullinated histone H3 (H3Cit-DNA) and other classical inflammatory markers to predict adverse events after STEMI. Methods This is a single-center retrospective cohort study of patients with STEMI undergoing primary percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI) from 2015 to 2019. We analyzed the association between serum H3Cit-DNA levels, double-stranded DNA, and classical inflammatory markers –such us interleukin (IL) 6 and 1β, TNF-α, and C-reactive protein (CRP)– on admission and the occurrence of major cardiovascular events (MACE), including death, reinfarction, urgent revascularization, or heart failure, after STEMI. Results A total of 487 patients were studied, of which 380 were men [78%]; mean [SD] age of patients was 63 [13] years, and median [95%CI] follow-up was 5.4 [5.2-5.5] years. Median [IQR] H3Cit level was 179.30 [105.30-281.47] ng/ml. No relevant association was found between H3Cit-DNA levels and 30-day mortality (OR, 1.03 [95%CI, 0.71-1.50], p = 0.861) or MACE (0.98 [0.72-1.32], p = 0.879), Killip class (0.95 [0.74-1.21], p = 0.664), or left ventricular ejection fraction (ref.cat. > 50%; < 35%, RRR 1.01 [95%CI, 0.74-1.38], p = 0.952; 35-50%, 1.26 [1.07-1.48], p = 0.005]. Adding CRP and IL-6 levels as covariates to a model based on classical risk factors significantly improved the prediction of MACE at 30 days after STEMI (IDI 0.13; NRI 0.32, p < 0.05). Conclusions Circulating levels of the NET marker H3Cit-DNA at the time of primary PCI were not predictive of cardiovascular events following STEMI. In contrast, the classical inflammatory markers CRP and interleukin-6 significantly enhanced the discriminative capacity of a clinical 30-day risk prediction model. The contact person (Belén Ruiz-Antorán) will be responsible for providing the data if necessary. Introduction Inflammation plays a pivotal role in the pathophysiology of atherosclerosis. In ST-elevation myocardial infarction (STEMI), the initial inflammatory response is typically triggered by plaque rupture and coronary occlusion at the culprit lesion site. This process encompasses the activation of polymorphonuclear neutrophils (PMN), the recruitment of monocytes, and the local release of pro-inflammatory mediators, such as interleukins (IL) [ 1 ]. The acute cytokine surge enhances neutrophil activation, promotes the release of granule enzymes such as myeloperoxidase (MPO) and catalase, and triggers an oxidative response [ 2 ]. During this phase of post-STEMI inflammation, processes that worsen the detrimental effects of inflammation –particularly involving key cytokines (e.g., IL-1 and IL-6) and PMN-induced neutrophil extracellular trap (NET) formation– are especially active, further amplifying their harmful impact [ 3 ]. Local inflammation evolves into a systemic response characterized by elevated inflammatory biomarkers, making early pro-inflammatory markers valuable tools for risk stratification after STEMI. Among the biomarkers of inflammation in atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease, C-reactive protein (CRP) is the most extensively studied. CRP, an acute-phase protein, is predominantly produced by hepatocytes under the influence of cytokines such as IL-6 and tumor necrosis factor-α [ 4 ]. Elevated CRP levels are associated with an increased risk of atherosclerotic cardiovascular events. Some but not all studies have found that serum СRР predicts the risk of a recurrent in-hospital cardiac event [ 5 ] or 30-day or long-term mortality after STEMI [ 6 , 7 ]. Interleukin-1β amplifies inflammation by promoting its own expression in various cell types and stimulating the production of IL-6 [ 8 ]. Blocking IL-1β and IL-6 receptors with specific antibodies has been shown to reduce circulating CRP levels [ 9 , 10 ]. Elevated IL-6 levels are associated with an increased risk of major adverse cardiovascular events (MACE) following myocardial infarction [ 11 ]. On the other hand, emerging experimental and clinical evidence indicates that the formation of NETs in coronary thrombosis exerts harmful effects. NETs are modified chromatin structures released by neutrophils in response to specific stimuli, bound to cytoplasmic and granular proteins. Although NETs play a protective role against pathogens, dysregulated NETs exhibit strong proinflammatory and prothrombotic properties. In patients with STEMI, the presence of NETs in coronary thrombi is associated with larger infarcts and worse short-term outcomes [ 12 – 14 ]. The NET-specific circulating marker, citrullinated histone H3 DNA complex (H3Cit-DNA), plays a central role in NET formation. A standardized detection method is now available [ 15 ], although its clinical applicability in this context remains uncertain. The primary objective of this study was to assess the utility of peripheral H3Cit-DNA levels and classical inflammatory markers in predicting adverse outcomes after STEMI.

molecular_mechanism_and_relationship.activity_type_context: ST-elevation myocardial infarction (STEMI), primary percutaneous coronary intervention (PPCI) outcomes, coronary thrombosis, and inflammation
molecular_mechanism_and_relationship.mechanism_description: Inflammation is central to STEMI pathophysiology, involving neutrophil activation and the release of pro-inflammatory mediators. Neutrophil extracellular trap (NET) formation in coronary thrombosis is linked to poor short-term prognosis and is directly related to infarct size and inversely related to ST-segment resolution. An acute cytokine surge enhances neutrophil activation, promotes granule enzyme release (e.g., myeloperoxidase and catalase), and triggers an oxidative response. Key cytokines (e.g., IL-1 and IL-6) and PMN-induced NET formation amplify harmful impacts, leading to a systemic inflammatory response. CRP, an acute-phase protein, is produced by hepatocytes under IL-6 and TNF- 1 influence. IL-1 2 amplifies inflammation by promoting its own expression and stimulating IL-6 production. Dysregulated NETs exhibit strong proinflammatory and prothrombotic properties. H3Cit is part of the PAD4-dependent NET formation pathway, which is central to neutrophil nuclear chromatin release, and a mutual induction of NETs and monocyte chemoattractant protein (MCP)-1 is associated with recurrent cardiovascular events and all-cause mortality after myocardial infarction.

dose_intensity_and_specificity.dose_comparison_summary: The study analyzed serum levels of markers on admission, focusing on the predictive utility of baseline biomarker levels rather than explicit dose-response effects or intensity comparisons of interventions. Serum H3Cit-DNA levels were associated with a mild to moderate reduction in LVEF (35 150%) compared to normal LVEF (> 50%) (RRR 1.26, p=0.005), but not with severe LVEF reduction (< 35%) (RRR 1.01, p=0.952). The methodology also involved analyzing inflammatory markers in relation to clinical outcomes with varying severity (e.g., Killip classification, LVEF categories).
dose_intensity_and_specificity.specificity_finding: The NET-specific marker H3Cit-DNA showed limited utility in predicting cardiovascular events (30-day mortality, MACE, Killip class, LVEF <35%) after STEMI, potentially due to issues with assay specificity and its role only in PAD4-dependent NET formation. Furthermore, commercial antibodies against H3Cit and ELISA kits for NET detection have 'highly questionable' specificity. dsDNA is a non-specific marker of NETosis. In contrast, classical inflammatory markers CRP and IL-6 significantly enhanced the discriminative capacity of a clinical 30-day risk prediction model for MACE. Only coronary dsDNA was independently associated with in-hospital MACE, suggesting local specificity.

clinical_implication_and_population.target_population: The study included 487 patients (78% male, mean age 63 [SD 13] years, 14% with history of coronary artery disease) with ST-elevation myocardial infarction (STEMI) who presented within 12 hours of symptom onset and underwent primary percutaneous coronary intervention (PPCI). Patients admitted more than 12 hours after symptom onset or with insufficient/lost serum samples were excluded.
clinical_implication_and_population.health_implication: The study aimed to improve the prediction of major cardiovascular events (MACE), including death, reinfarction, urgent revascularization, or heart failure, and 30-day mortality after STEMI. It also assessed associations with Killip classification and left ventricular ejection fraction (LVEF). The findings offer potential for improved risk stratification and guiding decision-making, particularly in identifying patients who might benefit from inflammation-targeted therapies during the early stages of STEMI.
clinical_implication_and_population.risk_classification: The study demonstrated diagnostic utility and prognostic value for risk stratification after STEMI. CRP and IL-6 significantly enhanced the discriminative ability of a 30-day STEMI clinical risk prediction model for MACE, improving risk stratification over models based solely on classical risk factors. In contrast, H3Cit-DNA showed limited diagnostic and prognostic utility for predicting MACE, mortality, Killip class, or most LVEF categories.

biomarker_reliability_and_future_focus.reliability_assessment: Circulating levels of the NET marker H3Cit-DNA were not predictive of cardiovascular events following STEMI, indicating limited utility and reliability. This unreliability is attributed to technical issues, large enzyme-dependent batch variability, instability in plasma, and poor antibody specificity of commercial assays. The specificity of commercial ELISA kits for MPO-DNA complexes is 'highly questionable', and dsDNA is a non-specific marker. Conversely, classical inflammatory markers C-reactive protein (CRP) and interleukin-6 (IL-6) demonstrated significant prognostic value and enhanced the discriminative capacity of clinical risk prediction models, suggesting higher reliability. Their high detectability (CRP 80%, IL-6 41%) further supports their utility. TNF 1 and IL-1 2 showed low detectability (12% and 8%), limiting their utility.
recommended_alternatives: A new H3Cit-DNA assay using highly specific monoclonal antibodies and semisynthetic nucleosomes (H3R2,8,17Cit) as calibration standards (as developed by Th 1lin et al.) is recommended for accurate and reliable quantification in human plasma. The incorporation of CRP and IL-6 into clinical practice is recommended, potentially to select patients for inflammation-targeted therapies.
